sections.skill: Tell transcription from speech generation and check transcripts

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: What does transcription do?

choices.text: Turns spoken audio into written words
Turns written words into a spoken voice that can read an article aloud to listeners

questions.correct_answer: Turns spoken audio into written words
questions.intro: Two audio tasks run in opposite directions. TRANSCRIPTION, also called SPEECH-TO-TEXT, turns spoken audio into written words, for example meeting notes or captions. SPEECH GENERATION, also called TEXT-TO-SPEECH, turns written words into spoken audio, for example a voice reading an article aloud. Transcripts can contain errors: misheard words ("wreck a nice beach" for "recognize speech"), wrong names, missing words when people talk over each other, and wrong SPEAKER LABELS that say who said what. Before relying on a transcript, check names, numbers and key statements against the recording.

sections.skill: Compare transcription and speech generation with a court reporter and a narrator

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: A court reporter is like which task?
questions.intro: A COURT REPORTER listens to people talking and types every word: sound in, text out. That is like transcription. An audiobook NARRATOR reads a written book aloud: text in, sound out. That is like speech generation. A court reporter can mishear a name or mix up who spoke, which is why records are checked. A narrator can mispronounce a word, but the book's text stays the same.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: Which recording is most likely to produce transcript errors?

choices.text: A quiet room with one person speaking slowly and clearly into a good microphone
A noisy room with people talking over each other

questions.correct_answer: A noisy room with people talking over each other
questions.intro: Transcription errors grow with noise, accents the system heard less often in training, fast speech, technical words and crosstalk. A transcript that looks clean may have quietly dropped a sentence or swapped "can" with "can't." For anything that matters, such as meeting decisions, quotes for an article or medical instructions, listen to the important parts again. Also ask permission before recording people; rules about recording consent differ by place.
